comingSoonShell.body:
This experience is being carefully prepared.
Please come back to visit.

archive.title: Choose a culture to carry.
archive.subtitleAll: Each one is disappearing a little faster than the last.

kiriko.description: Cut glass craft refracting light into delicate geometric patterns.
kiriko.problem: Only a handful of workshops remain.

washi.description: Handmade paper scooped from fibres of the kōzo tree.
washi.problem: Fewer than twenty artisans remain in some villages.

bingata.description: Stencil-and-resist dye craft of the Ryūkyū court; vivid tropical motifs.
bingata.problem: Few young craftsmen are learning the multi-stage stencil and resist technique.

hanabi.description: Traditional Japanese fireworks blooming as chrysanthemums in the night sky.
hanabi.problem: Master pyrotechnicians (花火師) are aging, and shrinking communities can no longer fund summer festivals.

lantern.description: Paper lanterns lit with a single flame, carried through summer streets.
lantern.problem: Hand-shaped washi lanterns are losing makers as plastic replicas spread.

taiko.description: Japanese drum at the heart of festivals, signalling gods and seasons.
taiko.problem: Local taiko troupes are losing players as villages depopulate.

sensu.description: Folding fan whose pleated washi cools the air and frames a private gesture.
sensu.problem: Master fan-makers are aging without successors.

tsugaru-nuri.description: 48-step lacquer with multi-color layers polished to reveal speckled 唐塗 patterns.
tsugaru-nuri.problem: Two-month process per piece; only about 30 active masters remain in Hirosaki.

nanbu-tekki.description: Cast-iron kettles with regular 霰文 raised pattern; iron leaching mellows the tea.
nanbu-tekki.problem: Foundries are closing as gas and electric stoves replace traditional charcoal kettles.

magewappa.description: Bent Akita cedar boxes stitched with cherry-bark thread; antibacterial and feather-light.
magewappa.problem: Akita cedar supply is dwindling; only about eleven master craftsmen remain.

mashiko-yaki.description: Rustic pottery with four traditional glazes; central to Hamada Shōji's mingei movement.
mashiko-yaki.problem: Younger potters are scarce; only about 250 kilns remain active versus around 600 a generation ago.

tsubame-sanjo.description: One copper sheet hammered tens of thousands of times into a seamless vessel.
tsubame-sanjo.problem: Younger metalsmiths are rare; world-class work, but the master pool is aging.

wajima-nuri.description: 124-step lacquerware with 沈金 and 蒔絵 gold decoration; Noto's earthquake-stricken treasure.
wajima-nuri.problem: The 2024 Noto Peninsula earthquake devastated workshops; recovery remains uncertain.

echizen-uchihamono.description: 700-year forging tradition; 二枚広げ + 廻し鋼着け produces thin, resilient blades.
echizen-uchihamono.problem: Industrial knives dominate the market; only about 30 active forges remain.

bizen-yaki.description: Unglazed pottery — fire and ash from 14-day firings create unique 景色 patterns.
bizen-yaki.problem: Long firing cycles are unprofitable; many young potters move to faster glazed styles.

kumano-fude.description: Premium calligraphy and makeup brushes; 80% domestic share, world brand-supplier.
kumano-fude.problem: Demand for lower-skill makeup brushes is falling; the calligraphy market is shrinking.

awa-odori.description: 400-year-old summer festival dance with a two-beat rhythm; about 1.3 million visitors a year.
awa-odori.problem: Younger ren are shrinking; pandemic-era cancellations broke continuity.

hakata-ningyo.description: Hand-painted bisque clay dolls; 目入れ (eye-painting) gives them their soul.
hakata-ningyo.problem: Modern decor demand is falling; only about 50 master craftsmen remain.

arita-yaki.description: Japan's first porcelain — white body with iconic cobalt 染付 underglaze.
arita-yaki.problem: Many small kilns have closed, competing with mass-produced imports.

step1.heading: Split bamboo into fan ribs
step1.hint: Split a single bamboo evenly into 13 thin ribs. Tap to cleave one strand at a time.

step2.heading: Fold the washi mountain-and-valley
step2.hint: Alternate mountain and valley folds. Each tap adds the next crease. Once accordioned, the paper becomes the fan face.

step3.heading: Paint the fan paper
step3.hint: Paint freely with ink or colour on the folded washi. Follow the creases or ignore them — your choice.

step4.heading: Set the rivet, open the fan
step4.hint: Slide the bamboo ribs into the paper and lock with the kaname rivet. Finally, drag to open the fan slowly.

step1.heading: Which warimono pattern?
step1.hint: A pyrotechnician first decides what to bloom. Both the stars and the shell are crafted around this pattern.

step2.heading: Layer colours onto the {pattern} stars
step2.hint: Coat tiny seeds with layered gunpowder + pigments. They burn outermost-first, so the last colour you add blooms first. Stack a colour twice to make it burn longer.

step3.heading: Pick the shell size
step3.hint: Pack your stars into a shell and wrap kraft paper around it. Thicker wrap = larger bloom.

step1.heading: Slice Akita cedar to 0.7mm
step1.hint: Glide the plane sideways along the grain. Shavings rise and a thin sheet emerges.

step2.heading: Soften fibres in hot water
step2.hint: 30 minutes at 90°C. The cedar prepares to bend in the steam. Tap to fast-forward.

step3.heading: Wrap around the form while warm
step3.hint: Pull both ends to meet the central form. Once cooled the shape locks in.

step4.heading: Stitch the seam with cherry bark
step4.hint: Thread thin strips of mountain-cherry bark through 5 stitch points. Akita's cherry bark is a proud traditional material in itself.

step1.heading: Knead the clay, build koshi
step1.hint: Kneading expels air and evens grain. The clay's quality decides the vessel's.

step2.heading: Throw the form on the wheel
step2.hint: Lift the form with your fingers as the wheel turns. Centre it and the rest is dialogue.

step3.heading: Pick from the four traditional glazes
step3.hint: Dip the glaze. The kiln's chemistry then reveals its colour.

step4.heading: Fire in the climbing kiln
step4.hint: 24 hours in the noborigama. Fire and ash collide to paint the keshiki landscape.

stir.hint: Trace circles in the water to loosen the kōzo fibres.

beat.hint: Beat the bundle with a wooden mallet.

scoop.hint: Rock the bamboo screen side to side to layer the fibres.

press.hint: Press and hold to squeeze the water out.

dry.hint: Let it dry in the sunlight.

rokuro.hint: Throw hiyose clay on the wheel — its iron content yields Bizen's signature colour after firing.

kamaire.hint: Where you place the piece in the kiln decides its keshiki. Position is part of the work.

shosei.hint: 10–14 days of firing. The accidents of ash, flame and heat compose the keshiki.

kashoku.hint: Read the finished keshiki. The same piece can never be made twice.

kashitsu.hint: Heat the kashitsu hearth to 1100°C. When the steel glows white-hot, that is the signal to strike.

tanzo.hint: Hammer it out. The nimaihiroge double-spread is a hallmark of the Chiyozuru lineage.

yakiire.desc: Quench in water — locks in the hamon
yakiire.hint: Quench in water → tempering hardens the steel. The hamon wave of a master blade is born here.

togi.hint: Sharpen on natural stone. The hamon pattern is co-authored by the quench and the sharpening.
